title: Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle
full_review:
Just when you thought Hollywood had scraped the bottom of the lowbrow-idea barrel, a movie comes along which reveals a trap door to the cask. With a running time of 87 minutes, "Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle" (New Line), a vulgar, mindless road-comedy with a self-summarizing title, is about an hour and a half too long.

To make a dumb story short, the, er, plot can be boiled down to a baby-burger-sized synopsis: Two toked-up stoners drive around New Jersey in search of fast-food nirvana.

John Cho plays uptight milquetoast Harold Lee, a low-level Asian-American investment banker who refuses to be confrontational, even when his Caucasian colleagues dump all their work on him. Kal Penn plays the mellow half of the titular team, Kumar Patel, a Hindi slacker who, despite having aced his med school entrance exams, intentionally blows his entrance interviews as a way of avoiding the specter of responsibility while sticking it to his physician father.

During a Friday night pot-smoking session, Harold and Kumar develop a severe case of the munchies. A commercial advertising White Castle hamburgers sends them into a mouthwatering frenzy and into Harold's car where they make a pact: White Castle or bust, even if it means driving all night.

Their adventure through the wilds of the Garden State is beset with mishaps, including run-ins with a pair of libidinous Princeton coeds with irritable bowels, a "born-again" cretin with puss-oozing boils and a kinky wife, a rabid raccoon, an escaped cheetah and Neil Patrick Harris -- of "Doogie Howser" fame -- who makes a what-was-he-thinking cameo playing himself.

As directed by Danny Leiner, "Harold & Kumar" is peppered with pretensions of social commentary about race and identity, but it seems like the only race this flick is concerned with is the race to the bottom -- a downward dash Leiner has already competed in with "Dude, Where's My Car?," his previous contribution to the canon of bar-lowering cinema. Despite its multicultural musings, the movie is a melting pot of gross-out scatological gags and lewd frat-house humor.

However, while the film uses comedy to address issues of ethnic and cultural stereotypes, it seems to exclude religion from its sensitivity purview. Throughout the movie, sacred objects are employed as sight gags, including using a traditional Jewish shofar as a marijuana bong, using a menorah as a cigarette repository, and adorning a doorway mezuza with a naked woman. In a display of equal-opportunity offensiveness, the film contains a lewd scene where Harold and Kumar try to have sex with another man's wife while surrounded by pictures and statues of the Virgin Mary.

Sadly, White Castle not only apparently approved of the script, but inducted the film's two leads into its "Cravers Hall of Fame."

White Castle itself should be inducted into a hall of shame for attempting to capitalize on some free Hollywood publicity by endorsing a film which promotes, as somehow humorous, smoking marijuana and getting behind the wheel of a car. The supposedly family-friendly franchise's Web site boasts of White Castle's "consistent history of high quality and great taste." So much for consistency.

Contrary to the movie's -- and White Castle's -- slogan, this kind of cinematic junk food is not what most viewers are craving.
Due to recurring drug use, two instances of frontal nudity, much rough and crude language, as well as strong sexual and bathroom humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
